newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan rejects oil monopoly's new price system.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan rejects oil monopoly's new price system.

text.p: Taiwan's Commission of National Corporations has rejected Chinese Petroleum Corp's proposed floating price system just two weeks before it was to take effect, the state oil monopoly said on Tuesday.

The commission, which oversees Taiwan's state enterprises, sent the proposal back with a list of questions and concerns about the proposed system's fairness to consumers, a Chinese Petroleum official told Reuters.
"The commission wants Chinese Petroleum to explain how the new pricing system will fairly reflect our oil import costs," the official said by telephone.

Analysts said the commission appeared to be worried that the system would allow Chinese Petroleum to set prices at highly profitable levels without making the price-setting process fully transparent to regulators and consumers.
Under the proposed system, retail petroleum prices would be adjusted every two weeks on the basis of import costs, rather than a few times a year as is currently done, executives said.
The new system was designed to fully reflect even minor fluctuations in the international oil market, they said.
Chinese Petroleum was likely to revise its proposal and resubmit it in 1997, the official said.
Commission officials were not available for immediate comment.

Under regulations adopted in 1996, Chinese Petroleum's monopoly will end in early 1998 when the first phase of a US$9 billion refinery being built by would-be competitor Formosa Plastics group enters production.
Chinese Petroleum's oil import costs averaged US$17.76 per barrel in May, higher than the $15.26 budgeted for the period but lower than April's $18.74, company figures show.

Citing high crude costs and a growing budget deficit, Chinese Petroleum has boosted local prices by about 12 percent in 1997, with an average nine percent increase on January 1 and a further 2.97 percent rise on April 4.
Executives said added revenues were needed -- despite a general decline in world crude prices -- to cover an accumulated budgetary deficit for the fiscal year that ends June 30.
As of May, Chinese Petroleum had accumulated a deficit of T$15.196 billion for the current fiscal year.
